# oc-bifrost — bridge a V1 plugin onto OpenCode V2

Read `INSTALL.md` in the oc-bifrost repo and execute it. Summary of the contract:

## The failure this fixes

V2 hard-rejects V1 plugin modules:

```
Plugin must export a default definition with an id and an effect or setup function
```

## Procedure

1. `opencode --version` → must be `2.x`.
2. `opencode debug paths` → read the `config` line. **Use that path.** Never assume `~/.config/opencode`.
3. Move the legacy plugin out of any discovered plugin directory — `.opencode/legacy/<name>.ts`. A V1 file left in `.opencode/plugins/` is rejected before the bridge can see it.
4. Add the bridge to the config's `plugins` array — one entry; OpenCode resolves the package, no `npm i`:
   `{ "package": "@nathwn12/oc-bifrost", "options": { "plugins": ["<one specifier>"] } }`
   The specifier is exactly one of three paths:
   - `github:<owner>/<repo>[@<ref>][#<path>]` — **the advertised, default route**, by source (requires oc-bifrost 0.4.0 or later; releases 0.3.0 and below cannot mount it).
     The first fetch downloads a plugin from GitHub and EXECUTES it with the host process's full user
     rights — by source means trusting the publisher. A cold cache refuses by default and names both
     opt-ins: `"trustRemote": true` on the bridge entry, or `OC_BIFROST_TRUST=github` in the
     environment. A warm, hash-verified cache then loads with no re-consent and no network; the mount
     report always prints the resolved commit, the digest, and the host-rights line. An offline cold
     cache fails closed and names the pre-warm path.
   - `preset:rtk` - optional offline / no-fetch fallback, for air-gapped hosts (needs the `rtk` binary on `PATH`)
   - a local path - `./.opencode/legacy/<name>.ts` (project) or an absolute path (global)
   Option keys: `provision` - `"host"` (default) junctions a fetched snapshot's declared
   dependencies from the shared OpenCode npm cache (zero network), `"npm"` adds an
   `npm install --no-save` fallback, `"off"` disables provisioning (`OC_BIFROST_PROVISION`
   sets the mode when the option is omitted; an explicit option wins). `wireTui` (default
   `false`) adds a `tui.tsx` wrapper and a `file://` plugins entry in cli.json after a
   `github:` snapshot mounts (`OC_BIFROST_WIRE_TUI=1` opts in; snapshot layouts only).
5. Restart. Confirm `loading plugin` with no `LoadError`, and read the printed report.
6. Verify with a **side effect**, not the report: trigger one real tool call and assert the plugin's observable behaviour actually happened.

## Matrix levels

- `full` — bridged, write-back proven (`tool.execute.before`, `shell.env`, `chat.headers`, `permission.ask`, `dispose`).
- `partial` — bridged with a stated loss (`tool.execute.after`, `chat.params`, `chat.message`, `tool.definition`, `tool`, `event`, the `experimental.*` session hooks).
- `unsupported` — refused out loud: `config`, `auth`, `provider`, `command.execute.before`, `experimental.provider.small_model`, `experimental.compaction.autocontinue`, `experimental.text.complete`.

If the plugin depends on an `unsupported` hook, report it as a **port candidate** — never as a bridged success.

## Guardrails

- Config edits may be owned by another writer agent — delegate on the first denial; never route around it.
- Never silently enable `trustRemote` for a `github:` plugin: it executes publisher code with the
  host process's full user rights. Surface that decision to the human.
- Never permanently change the host environment to make a test pass.
- Use the bare `"@nathwn12/oc-bifrost"` entry. It tracks the newest published release and never names a
  version that does not exist between a bump and its publish; add `@<version>` only to hold a known
  published release. If the plugin cache settles on a stale version, run `opencode plugin check`, or
  delete `~/.cache/opencode/npm/@nathwn12/oc-bifrost@latest` and reload.
- For any read of the OpenCode source, cite `file:line`.

oc-bifrost

Run V1-era OpenCode plugins on V2: supported hooks bridge, the rest refuse out loud.

## Install Add one entry to the `plugins` array in your `opencode.jsonc` and restart OpenCode. OpenCode fetches the package itself; you run no install command: ```jsonc { "plugins": [ { "package": "@nathwn12/oc-bifrost", "options": { "plugins": ["github:obra/superpowers"], "trustRemote": true } } ] } ``` ## Use it Name the plugins you want in the `plugins` option. Accepts four sources: a GitHub snapshot, a registry package, a local path, and the bundled offline `preset:rtk`. A cold `github:` cache refuses until you set `trustRemote`, then pins the snapshot by commit and digest. Registry packages, local paths and `preset:rtk` need no remote trust. The bridge takes 24 V1 hooks: 5 bridge fully, 10 bridge with a stated loss, and 9 refuse by design. A lost hook is named, never silently dropped. Every load prints `full`, `partial`, or `unsupported` per hook and mirrors it to a durable report file, because the host discards stdout in service and stdio modes. On each start, read the mount report so a `partial` or `unsupported` verdict tells you exactly what changed before you blame your own plugin. ### Configure it All settings live in the `options` object of the entry above: | Option | Effect | | --- | --- | | `plugins` | The V1 plugins to mount. Accepts `github:`, registry, local path, and `preset:` sources. | | `trustRemote` | Allows a cold GitHub fetch. Without it the bridge refuses instead of fetching unverified code. | | `provision` | How snapshot dependencies are resolved: from the host store, an `npm install --no-save` fallback, or no action. | A stranded-file scan warns when a V1 plugin file sits in a discovery directory the host would reject before the bridge runs. ## Requirements - OpenCode 2.2.6 or newer. - Node 22 or later. - The npm registry must be reachable for the first fetch of a registry or GitHub plugin. ## Status **Unverified** — as-is, use at your own risk. ## Links - [Issues](https://github.com/nathwn12/oc-collections/issues) - [Releases](https://github.com/nathwn12/oc-collections/releases) - [Guide](https://github.com/nathwn12/oc-collections/blob/main/packages/oc-bifrost/docs/GUIDE.md) - [Third-party notices](https://github.com/nathwn12/oc-collections/blob/main/packages/oc-bifrost/THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md) - [MIT licence](https://github.com/nathwn12/oc-collections/blob/main/LICENSE)

### Why it is vendored

Upstream's own installer documents writing this file to
`~/.config/opencode/plugins/rtk.ts` (see upstream `hooks/opencode/README.md`). That is a plugin
**discovery** directory. OpenCode V2 loads a bare `.ts` file found there *directly* and hard-rejects
a V1 module — before oc-bifrost can ever see it. So the documented install path is precisely the one
that breaks.

Vendoring lets the `preset:rtk` spec mount the same bytes from a location V2 never scans.

Because the file is unmodified, Apache-2.0's "state your changes" clause is not triggered. The full
license text travels alongside as `rtk-LICENSE`.

### Updating this copy

The pin lives in **three** places that must never drift: the bytes in `vendor/rtk.ts`, the
provenance in `vendor/rtk.meta.json` (and the table above), and the version in `src/preset.ts`.
`test/provenance.test.js` fails the suite if they diverge.

**Primary path — the updater.**

> **Requires a source checkout.** It rewrites `src/preset.ts` (the pin), `vendor/rtk.ts` and this file —
> and `src/` is not part of the published package. The copy that ships inside the npm tarball is
> included for auditability, not to be run from `node_modules`.

```sh
npm run vendor:update                          # latest upstream release (network)
npm run vendor:update -- --ref v0.51.0         # a specific tag
npm run vendor:update -- --from-file ./rtk.ts --expect-sha256 <hex>   # offline / CI
npm run vendor:update -- --dry-run             # show the writes, change nothing
```

It resolves the tag, downloads `hooks/opencode/rtk.ts`, then **verifies the bytes against an
independent record** before writing anything:

- **Network path** — our computed git blob must equal GitHub's own recorded blob id for the file
  at that ref (the contents API's `sha`).
- **Offline path** (`--from-file`) — there is no third party to ask, so an independently obtained
  digest is required: `--expect-sha256 <hex>` or `--expect-blob <sha1>`. Without one, a real run
  refuses to write. `--dry-run` still runs but says loudly that no verification was possible.

A cheap sanity check (not a verification gate) rejects content that is empty, larger than 64 KiB,
an HTML error page, or has no source shape at all — the updater writes bytes it downloaded.

It then writes `vendor/rtk.ts`, refreshes `vendor/rtk.meta.json`, rewrites the table above,
updates the pin in `src/preset.ts`, and runs `npm run check`. If the check fails it prints the
exact revert: `git checkout -- vendor src/preset.ts`.

**Fallback — manual.**

1. Fetch `hooks/opencode/rtk.ts` at a new tag.
2. Record the new byte length, git blob, and sha256 in the table above **and** in `vendor/rtk.meta.json`.
3. Update the pinned version in `src/preset.ts`.
4. Keep `rtk-LICENSE` current; Apache-2.0 permits redistribution with the license retained.

# INSTALL — agent-first

**You are the agent. This page is written for you to execute.** The human says *"set up oc-bifrost for my `<plugin>`"* — you do the rest and report.

Do not hand the human a wall of steps. Do them, then report: what you changed, what you verified, what you could not.

## 0. Preflight (always)

1. Confirm the host is OpenCode V2 at the bridge's floor: `opencode --version` → expect `2.2.6` or newer.
2. Locate the config in use: `opencode debug paths` → read the `config` line. **Never assume `~/.config/opencode`** — respect the reported path. If `OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR` is set, that is the config root.
3. Confirm you may write there. The global config directory is often owned by a stricter writer agent. If your write is denied, **hand the edit to that writer; never reword the path or route it through a shell**.

## 1. Add the bridge entry

The bridge is one entry in the config's `plugins` array. OpenCode resolves and installs the npm
package itself — there is no separate `npm i` step:

```jsonc
{
  "plugins": [
    {
      "package": "@nathwn12/oc-bifrost",
      "options": {
        "plugins": ["<exactly one specifier — one of the four paths below>"],
        "strict": false,
        "verbose": true
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

### 1a. Choose the version form — then verify what resolved

**Use the bare name:** `"@nathwn12/oc-bifrost"` - the default. It tracks the newest published release.
A pinned entry (`"@nathwn12/oc-bifrost@<version>"`) names a version that does not exist between a bump
and its publish, so use a pin only to hold a known published release. State the form you used in your report.

After adding the entry, **verify the resolved version — do not assume it**:

```sh
opencode plugin check     # re-resolves online
opencode plugin list      # shows what is actually loaded
```

If the resolved version is wrong or stale, delete
`~/.cache/opencode/npm/@nathwn12/oc-bifrost@latest` and reload - the bare entry re-resolves.

### 1b. Install route - npm only

The npm registry is the only supported install route. Every fix on `main` releases to npm as the next patch (MEASURED: WORKS). The entry (bare name):

```jsonc
{
  "plugins": [
    {
      "package": "@nathwn12/oc-bifrost",
      "options": {
        "plugins": ["<exactly one specifier - one of the four paths below>"],
        "strict": false,
        "verbose": true
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

The npm tarball ships the compiled `dist/` (the `prepublishOnly` step builds it before packing), so the registry entry always has a working entry point. Git and local-clone installs are not supported routes.

Use the package name (`"@nathwn12/oc-bifrost"`): it resolves through npm and honours the package's `exports`. A local directory path will not work — OpenCode looks for `index.js`/`index.ts` at the directory root, ignores `exports`, and drops the entry silently (no load, no error, no log line). This is a real limitation, not a supported route.

## 2. Mount the legacy plugin — one of four paths

| # | Path | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `github:` (advertised / default) | the plugin's source lives in a GitHub repo — online fetch |
| 2 | `preset:rtk` (offline fallback, optional) | no network — GitHub unreachable, or an air-gapped host |
| 3 | local file (fallback) | the plugin is a file on disk |
| 4 | registry package | the plugin is published on the npm registry (bare name, or `npm:` / `pnpm:` / `bun:`) |

Pick exactly one per plugin. Anything outside those four forms is refused out loud with the
accepted-forms message — the bridge never guesses which source you meant.

### Path 1 — `github:` (advertised / default, online)

`github:<owner>/<repo>[@<ref>][#<path>]` — e.g. `github:obra/superpowers`.

**Snapshot-first.** The ref resolves to a commit once, at first fetch (the repository's
default branch when no `@<ref>`), then the **repository tarball** is downloaded from
codeload **at that resolved commit** and materialized as a whole tree — sibling files
exist beside the entry file, so `github:obra/superpowers` reads its own `skills/`.

- **Caps:** 16 MiB compressed · 64 MiB uncompressed · 5000 files. A breach never
  truncates — it degrades (below) loudly.
- **Hostile archives are refused outright, never materialized:** path-traversal,
  absolute/`..` escapes, NUL/backslash names, duplicate paths. A link or device entry
  refuses the snapshot too. Nothing hostile is cached and nothing is executed.
- **Loud single-file fallback.** An over-cap, malformed, or candidate-less snapshot
  mounts via the old one-file fetch — the mount note says loudly that sibling files are
  **NOT** available and a plugin that reads them by relative path is inert. The
  downgrade is never silent.
- No `#<path>` → `hooks/opencode/<repo>.ts`, `hooks/opencode/index.ts`, `plugin.ts`, and
  `index.ts` are probed in order inside the materialized tree. Pass `#<path>` when the
  plugin lives elsewhere; a failed probe lists every path it tried.
- First load fetches once into the shared user cache at
  `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/opencode/oc-bifrost/github/v2/<id>/` (default:
  `~/.cache/opencode/oc-bifrost/github/v2/<id>/`; the tree sits at `…/v2/<id>/tree/`)
  and records the sha256 of the tarball **and** the entry file — trust on first use.
  Later loads from any project verify the cached bytes against that record with zero
  network; a mismatch refuses loudly. A flat pre-snapshot cache at `…/github/<id>/` is
  ignored with a warning (it cannot provide sibling files) and re-fetched with the same
  one-time consent.

**Consent gate — the first fetch is an explicit, informed opt-in.** The first fetch
downloads a repository snapshot from GitHub and executes its entry file with the host
process's full user rights. Mounting by source is trusting the publisher; the recorded
sha256 pins those bytes afterwards, it does not vouch for them. A cold cache refuses by
default, before anything is fetched or executed, and names exactly what would be
downloaded and both opt-ins:

```text
[oc-bifrost] refusing to fetch "github:obra/superpowers" (cold cache, first use): the first fetch would download the repository snapshot at the resolved commit (up to 16777216 compressed bytes), including one of, in order: hooks/opencode/superpowers.ts, hooks/opencode/index.ts, plugin.ts, index.ts from https://github.com/obra/superpowers at the repository's default branch (resolved at fetch time) and EXECUTE its entry file with this host process's full user rights. First-use fetching is opt-in, per oc-bifrost entry: set options.trustRemote: true, or set the environment variable OC_BIFROST_TRUST=github. Nothing was fetched and nothing was executed. A warm (hash-verified) cache never needs this consent.
```

- Opt in on the bridge entry, or via the environment:

  ```jsonc
  { "package": "@nathwn12/oc-bifrost", "options": { "trustRemote": true, "plugins": ["github:obra/superpowers"] } }
  ```

  `OC_BIFROST_TRUST=github` does the same from the environment; an explicit `trustRemote: false`
  wins over it.
- A warm, hash-verified cache needs no re-consent and no network.
- The mount report always prints the resolved commit, the digest, and the host-rights line
  (`…; executes with the host process's full user rights`) — the consent stays informed on every
  load.
- Offline or air-gapped: the cold-cache fetch fails closed —
  `Cold-cache fetching is fail-closed — oc-bifrost never falls back to another source. If this machine
  is offline or air-gapped, pre-warm the cache on a networked machine (run oc-bifrost once with
  opt-in) and copy its shared `oc-bifrost/github` cache directory across.`

> **Version gate.** `github:` requires **oc-bifrost 0.4.0 or later**; releases **0.3.0 and below**
> cannot mount it — on those, use path 2 (offline fallback) or path 3.

### Path 2 — `preset:rtk` (offline fallback, optional, bundled, zero-fetch)

`"plugins": ["preset:rtk"]` mounts the vendored `rtk-ai/rtk` plugin (`v0.50.0`, Apache-2.0).
Nothing is fetched and nothing is parked.

Prerequisite: the `rtk` binary (`>= 0.23.0`) on `PATH`. The preset probes before mounting and warns
loudly if it is missing (`strict: true` aborts). Install the binary once:

```sh
winget install rtk-ai.rtk        # Windows
brew install rtk                 # macOS / Linux
```

or take the release asset from [`rtk-ai/rtk`](https://github.com/rtk-ai/rtk/releases). Do **not**
`cargo install rtk` — the crates.io crate of that name is a different project.

Do **not** run `rtk init -g --opencode`: it writes `rtk.ts` into `<config>/plugins/`, a discovery
directory (see step 3).

### Path 3 — local file (fallback)

- Project install: `"plugins": ["./.opencode/legacy/<name>.ts"]` — a relative specifier resolves
  against the **session directory**, so it works only in the project that owns the file.
- Global install: park the file in `<config>/legacy/<name>.ts` and reference it by **absolute path**
  — e.g. `C:/Users/you/.config/opencode/legacy/rtk.ts`, or `/home/you/.config/opencode/legacy/rtk.ts`
  on macOS/Linux.

### Path 4 — registry package (bare name, or `npm:` / `pnpm:` / `bun:`)

`"plugins": ["oc-todo"]`, `"plugins": ["@scope/pkg@^1.0.0"]`, `"plugins": ["pkg@latest"]` — a bare
registry specifier, a range, or a dist-tag; a pinned exact version (`pkg@<version>`) is accepted too. The
same specifiers work behind an `npm:` / `pnpm:` / `bun:` prefix, which is stripped before the bare spec
is parsed and validated.

- **The host does not cover this, so the bridge installs the package itself.** The host installer
  drops `npm:` alias specs and ships no pnpm/bun installer. The bridge spawns a manager -
  `bun add --exact <bare>` first (the host runs on bun), `npm install --no-save --legacy-peer-deps
  <bare>` as the fallback - through the current JS runtime with an argv array and no shell.
- **A cold install needs network; the warm cache needs none.** The installed tree lands in a
  bifrost-owned cache at `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/opencode/oc-bifrost/registry/<id>/` (default
  `~/.cache/opencode/oc-bifrost/registry/<id>/`) beside a `meta.json` provenance record. A warm
  entry whose record matches the requested spec loads with zero spawns and no network; when the
  record names a different spec, the load refuses loudly.
- **The entry is the package's own declaration** - `exports` / `module` / `main` read from the
  installed `package.json` - and it must exist before import, or the mount fails loudly and nothing
  is mounted. The specifier is refused before anything is spawned if it carries control characters
  or shell metacharacters.
- **It mounts whatever it resolves to:** a V1 package bridges hook by hook, a `{id, setup}` V2 definition runs its
  native `setup` while an Effect-only `{id, effect}` definition is refused out loud for direct host mounting - the same shape-based routing as every other path.
- **`pnpm:` and `bun:` are aliases**, not real pnpm/bun installs: they install through the same
  spawned manager, and the mount note says so plainly rather than implying otherwise.
- The mount note names the installed version, the requested spec, the entry, and the manager that
  performed the install, and always ends with the host-rights line.

> **Version gate.** Registry specifiers require **oc-bifrost 1.6.0 or later**; releases **1.5.x and
> below** refuse them. On those, use path 1, 2, or 3.

## 3. Park the legacy plugins correctly

**A V1 plugin left in `.opencode/plugins/` is hard-rejected by V2 before the bridge can see it:**

```
Plugin must export a default definition with an id and an effect or setup function
```

Move it out of discovery — `legacy/` is the convention — and reference it from `options.plugins`:

- relative specifiers resolve against the **session directory** (project-local only)
- absolute paths work everywhere; a bare name (or an `npm:` / `pnpm:` / `bun:` specifier) is not a
  file - it is a registry mount, path 4 above
- the bridge warns at load when it finds a stranded V1 file in a discovery directory

### Global install (all projects)

The same rule applies with a sharper edge at the global config:

- Park the legacy plugin in `<config>/legacy/<name>.ts` — **never** in `<config>/plugin/`
  or `<config>/plugins/`. Those two are discovery directories: a bare `.ts` file there is
  loaded directly and hard-rejected before the bridge can see it.
- Reference it by **absolute path**. The bridge resolves relative specifiers against the
  session directory, so `./legacy/rtk.ts` only works in the one project that owns that file.

> **Known landmine.** Some plugins ship their own installer — `rtk init -g --opencode` writes
> the plugin straight into `<config>/plugins/`. Because that directory is scanned, the
> installer *breaks* the host instead of wiring the bridge. Park the file in `legacy/` and
> reference it from `options.plugins` instead.

## 4. Verify (do not skip — this is the deliverable)

1. Restart the host so the config reloads.
2. Trigger one real tool call (any shell command is enough).
3. Confirm:
   - the load log contains `loading plugin` for the bridge entrypoint, and **no** `LoadError`;
   - the bridge printed a per-plugin report: `mounted v1:<id>`, then a row per hook.
4. If the plugin's behaviour is observable (a rewritten command, a marker file, a toast), assert on the **side effect**, not on the report. The report says what was registered; only the side effect says it executed.
5. **Strongest check — read the host's spawn log.** Run a host with `--print-logs` and grep for `spawning process`. The logged `args` are the command that *actually executed*, after every `tool.execute.before` rewrite — the host's own record, not an inference:

   ```pwsh
   opencode run --standalone --print-logs --format json "run exactly: git status --porcelain"
   # then:
   Select-String -Path <captured output> -Pattern 'spawning process'
   ```

   A bridged rewrite shows up as e.g. `rtk git status --porcelain`. Note the tool-call record
   still shows the *pre-rewrite* input, so the spawn log is the only place the real command is
   visible.

**Legend:** `full` = bridged with write-back · `partial` = bridged with a stated loss · `unsupported` = refused out loud (set `strict: true` to abort instead).

Remove the bridge entry from `plugins` and restart. Delete the corresponding entry under

if you want to remove a downloaded `github:` plugin. Nothing else was modified: the bridge writes
no state to the project.

State: path used (1, 2, 3, or 4) · config path touched · legacy plugin path · hooks mounted and their levels · the side effect you verified · anything `unsupported` the plugin depends on. If a hook the plugin needs is `unsupported`, say so plainly and do not claim success.

oc-bifrost guide

## How it works The bridge loads as one V2 plugin. Everything else — your V1 plugins — is data it mounts, not code you install. 1. **Resolve.** Each entry in `plugins` becomes one specifier: `github:/[@][#]`, a registry package name, a local path, or `preset:rtk`. A relative specifier resolves against the **session** directory, not against this plugin's own location. 2. **Fetch, if it is remote.** A `github:` specifier is cached under the shared OpenCode user cache and pinned by commit sha plus the entry file's sha256, verified again on every later load. A cold cache refuses until you consent. A registry package is installed into its own cache directory the same way. 3. **Classify by shape, not by name.** A V1 hook factory, a V1 module, and a V2 `{ id, setup }` definition are told apart by what they export. V2 definitions mount natively with the host context; V1 shapes go through the bridge. 4. **Bridge hook by hook.** Every hook the plugin declares is looked up in the compatibility matrix below. `full` and `partial` hooks are wired to their V2 destination. `unsupported` hooks are refused out loud. 5. **Report.** One line per hook, per plugin, on every load. ### The bridge contract 24 V1 hooks. `full` means the V1 semantics survive intact. `partial` means it bridges and the report names exactly what changed. `unsupported` means it is refused by design and the plugin keeps running without it. | V1 hook | Level | Where it lands, or why it does not | | --- | --- | --- | | `tool.execute.before` | full | `ctx.tool.hook("execute.before")` — mutable `event.input` with write-back. | | `shell.env` | full | `ctx.shell.hook("create.before")` — merges into `event.env`. | | `chat.headers` | full | `ctx.session.hook("model.request")` — writes request headers. | | `permission.ask` | full | `ctx.permission.hook("evaluate")` — writes the evaluate effect. | | `dispose` | full | The setup cleanup return. | | `tool.execute.after` | partial | `ctx.tool.hook("execute.after")`. `result.output`/`metadata` and `error.message` write back; V1 `output.title` is dropped on both branches because V2 has no title field. | | `chat.params` | partial | Fans out to the `context`, `compaction`, `generate` and `title` session hooks. A non-numeric generation setting is warned about and never reaches the model request. | | `chat.message` | partial | `ctx.session.hook("prompt")` — writes prompt files, agents and skills. | | `tool.definition` | partial | Applied as a transform over a snapshot, because V2's editor is synchronous and the V1 hook is async. | | `tool` | partial | `ctx.tool.transform` editor `add`. | | `event` | partial | `ctx.event.subscribe()`. Terminal execution events are synthesised into the V1 `session.idle` envelope; other names and payloads pass through unchanged. | | `client.session.messages` | partial | `ctx.session.context({ sessionID })` — the **active** context after compaction, not the full transcript. | | `experimental.chat.system.transform` | partial | Fans out to the same four session hooks; untouched parts are preserved. | | `experimental.chat.messages.transform` | partial | Same fan-out. Non-text V1 parts land verbatim in `content`, because the V2 prompt contract admits only text, files, agents and skills. | | `experimental.session.compacting` | partial | `ctx.session.hook("compaction")` — `output.context` is appended to the system prompt; `output.prompt` is accepted and ignored, as the V2 result carries no prompt field. | | `client.session.children` | unsupported | V2 exposes no plugin-scoped child-session listing, and the plugin context carries no server address to ask over HTTP. | | `client.tui.showToast` | unsupported | A server plugin has no toast surface; `tui.toast.show` belongs to the TUI process. | | `config` | unsupported | V2 replaced one config hook with per-domain transforms of different semantics. | | `auth` | unsupported | V2 uses `ctx.integration.transform` plus the integration APIs. | | `provider` | unsupported | V2 uses `ctx.provider.transform` / `ctx.model.transform`. | | `command.execute.before` | unsupported | No one-to-one global V2 hook. | | `experimental.provider.small_model` | unsupported | No V2 equivalent. | | `experimental.compaction.autocontinue` | unsupported | No V2 equivalent. | | `experimental.text.complete` | unsupported | No V2 equivalent. | `strict: true` turns any `unsupported` row from a warning into a thrown error that aborts that plugin's setup. The default keeps mounting the rest. ### The mount report Every load writes a report. Each line is ` — ` under a `[oc-bifrost] ` header: ```text [oc-bifrost] github:acme/widget full tool.execute.before — mutable event.input + event.tool write-back full dispose — setup cleanup mounted v1:Widget — V1 named export (WidgetPlugin) mounted github:acme/widget — loaded from cache (commit 4f2a…, snapshot 2 files; entry sha256 765f… verified); executes with the host process's full user rights partial chat.params — mapped onto session context/compaction/generate/title generation options unsupported client.session.children — no plugin-scoped child listing; skipped ``` Four levels appear: `full`, `partial`, `unsupported`, and `mounted` (a plugin shape that mounted, with no hook verdict of its own). Console output is not enough on its own — the host discards stdout when it runs as a background service or a stdio server — so every line is mirrored to a file: ```text /opencode/oc-bifrost/report.log ``` The file appends across loads and rolls over at 256 KiB, so the newest report survives whole. Control characters are escaped before they land on disk. A sink failure is warned about once and never breaks a mount. ## Configuration One file, `oc-bifrost.jsonc`, in the OpenCode config directory. The directory resolves as `$OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR` when set, else `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/opencode`, else `~/.config/opencode` — the same root the host reports from `opencode debug paths`. An `options` key on the plugin entry wins key by key over the file. ```jsonc { // ~/.config/opencode/oc-bifrost.jsonc "plugins": ["github:obra/superpowers"], "trustRemote": true, "provision": "npm" } ``` | Key | Default | Effect | | --- | --- | --- | | `plugins` | unset | The specifiers to mount, one per entry. Nothing mounts until you list something. | | `trustRemote` | `false` | Consent for a cold `github:` cache to download and execute remote code. A warm, hash-verified cache needs no re-consent. | | `strict` | `false` | An `unsupported` hook or a failed entry aborts that plugin's setup instead of warning and mounting the rest. | | `verbose` | `true` | `false` silences the `partial` lines. `unsupported` lines and refusals still print. | | `freshness` | `"off"` | `"online"` checks the bundled `preset:rtk` against its upstream release after it mounts. | | `provision` | `"host"` | How a snapshot's dependencies are resolved: `"host"` uses the shared OpenCode npm cache, `"npm"` adds an `npm install --no-save` fallback for packages the host store lacks, `"off"` provisions nothing. An invalid value is a loud refusal naming the valid modes. | | `wireTui` | `false` | `true` wires a mounted `github:` snapshot's TUI entry into your `cli.json`. A tree with no TUI entry is a clean skip, not a failure. | Each key has an environment fallback, used only when the option and the file are both silent: | Variable | Opts in when | Effect | | --- | --- | --- | | `OC_BIFROST_TRUST` | exactly `github` | Same as `trustRemote: true`. Any other value is off. | | `OC_BIFROST_FRESHNESS` | exactly `online` | Same as `freshness: "online"`. | | `OC_BIFROST_PROVISION` | `host`, `npm`, or `off` | Same as `provision`. | | `OC_BIFROST_WIRE_TUI` | `1` or `true`, case-insensitive | Same as `wireTui: true`. | | `OC_BIFROST_REPORT` | any path | Overrides the report file location. `off` disables the file. | An explicit option always beats the environment, and an explicit `false` beats an opt-in variable. ## Commands The bridge has no CLI of its own. These are the host commands that verify it, and they are read-only: | Command | What it returns | | --- | --- | | `opencode plugin check` | Whether every configured plugin loads. Run it first: a specifier the host cannot resolve fails here, before the bridge sees it. | | `opencode plugin list` | The loaded plugins, including `@nathwn12/oc-bifrost`. | | `opencode debug paths` | The config, cache and state roots, which is how you find the file this guide names. | After a restart, the check you care about is the mount report, not the exit status of either command: ```text [oc-bifrost] preset:rtk full tool.execute.before — mutable event.input + event.tool write-back mounted v1:Rtk — V1 named export (RtkPlugin) ``` ## Troubleshooting **A `github:` plugin refuses with a consent error.** The cache is cold and `trustRemote` is not set. Set `"trustRemote": true` on that entry, or `OC_BIFROST_TRUST=github`. The refusal names the variable. **A mounted plugin refuses with a missing package.** Its dependencies are not in the host store. Set `"provision": "npm"` on that entry: the host junction is still attempted first, and the npm fallback covers what it lacks. **`preset:rtk` refuses.** It needs the `rtk` binary, at least `0.23.0`, on `PATH`. The report names the binary and the consequence. **A local plugin path refuses.** Relative specifiers resolve against the session directory, not this plugin's location. For a global install use an absolute path or `~/…`. V1 files parked in `plugin/` or `plugins/` are rejected by the host before the bridge runs — park them in `legacy/` instead. The stranded-file scan warns when it finds one. **A hook works on V1 and does nothing on V2.** Read its row above. If it is `partial`, the loss is named in the report line. If it is `unsupported`, there is no V2 destination to bridge to and no setting turns it on. **The report is missing.** The host discards stdout in service and stdio modes by design. Read the file, or set `OC_BIFROST_REPORT` to a path you can reach. **`strict: true` aborted the mount.** That is what it is for. Name the refused hook in the report, remove `strict`, and mount the rest — or drop the plugin. ## Limitations - The matrix above is the whole contract: 24 hooks. A hook outside it is never bridged, and the report covers the 24, not whatever else a plugin exports. - `client.session.messages` sees the active, post-compaction context only. The full transcript is not reachable from the V2 plugin facade. - `client.session.children` and `client.tui.showToast` cannot be bridged at all: one needs a server address the plugin context does not carry, the other lives in the TUI process. - Mounted remote plugins execute with the host process's full user rights. The pin proves the bytes did not change after the first fetch; it does not sandbox them. - The bridge does not fix a plugin's logic. It maps hooks; a V1 plugin that depended on a refused hook is still missing that behaviour. - The git ref install route for the bridge package itself fails host-side today. Use the npm route. - Windows and macOS/Linux both work only as far as OpenCode V2 itself does; the bridge makes no platform claim of its own. ## Links - Source: - Package: - Compatibility matrix: - Setup guide: [INSTALL.md](../INSTALL.md) - Verification record: [PROOF.md](../PROOF.md) - Issues: - Releases: - License: [LICENSE](../LICENSE)
